key_terms.meaning: The promise that data is readable only by those allowed to read it; broken by interception or a leak.
The promise that data has not been changed, deleted or forged by anyone not allowed to do so.
The promise that the service answers legitimate users when they ask; broken by flooding or destruction.
A sender cannot later deny a message; delivered by digital signatures and audit logs, not by secrecy alone.
A table listing each data item against each role or condition, marking who may read it.
An active attack in which the attacker inserts false data or a false identity into the system.
A cryptographic mechanism that binds a message to a key so any change is detectable and the signer cannot deny it.
The security service that decides, per request, whether this subject may perform this action on this object.
A potential cause of harm — a person, program or event that could exploit a weakness.
A weakness in design, code, configuration or people that a threat can use.
The sum of all points where an attacker can try to enter or extract data from a system.
Expected loss = likelihood of a threat exploiting a vulnerability × size of the resulting damage.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System; a public 0–10 score for the severity of one vulnerability.
Distributed denial of service; many machines flood one target at once so it cannot serve real users.
Man-in-the-middle; the attacker relays traffic between two parties, reading or altering it, while each side thinks it talks to the other.
The attacker captures a valid message and sends it again later to repeat its effect.
A virus that rewrites its own code on each infection so byte signatures no longer match.
Malware that encrypts or locks the victim's files and demands payment for the key.
Social engineering in which the attacker invents a believable role and story to justify a request.
A network of infected machines (bots) that obey one operator, usually through a command-and-control channel.

takeaways: Every security requirement you will meet is one of three promises: keep it secret, keep it correct, keep it reachable.
Attacks are what the enemy does, services are what you promise the user, and mechanisms are the tools that deliver the promise — keep the three words apart in an exam.
A threat alone causes no loss; loss happens only where a threat meets a vulnerability, and risk puts a number on that meeting.
Most network attacks reduce to three shapes: drown the service, sit in the middle of the conversation, or replay a captured message.
Malware is best classified by what it needs to spread — a host file, a live network, or a user's trust.
Social engineering cannot be patched, so defence is a trained habit backed by a technical control that stops the mistake becoming a breach.
A botnet is a rented army; the command-and-control channel with regular beacons is both its strength and the point where defenders can detect it.
CIA is not a checklist to tick once — each goal pulls against the others, and a design is a balance chosen for a stated threat model.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to use the standard classification vocabulary precisely — passive versus active attacks, services versus mechanisms, virus versus worm versus trojan — and then attach a concrete control to each named threat.

bank.q: Define the three CIA security goals. For a UPI payment app, give one concrete failure of each goal and name the goal being lost.
outline: Correct definition of confidentiality, integrity, availability
One realistic UPI example per goal (data leak, tampered amount, app down during festival rush)
Correctly names which goal each failure breaks
Mentions that authentication supports all three but is not itself one of them

bank.q: Distinguish between a security attack, a security service and a security mechanism. Give one example of each and show how they link.
outline: Attack = action that compromises security; service = guarantee offered to users; mechanism = tool or procedure that implements the service
Example attack: interception; example service: data confidentiality; example mechanism: encipherment
Clear statement that a mechanism counters an attack in order to deliver a service
One line on why confusing the terms leads to bad design

bank.q: Classify security attacks into passive and active categories with sub-types, and place interception, modification, fabrication and replay in the correct class.
outline: Passive: eavesdropping/interception, traffic analysis — goal is information, no change to data
Active: masquerade, replay, modification of messages, denial of service, fabrication
Correct placement of each named attack
Note that passive attacks are hard to detect, active attacks are easier to detect but harder to prevent

bank.q: Explain how a virus, a worm and a trojan differ in what they need to spread and what damage they do.
outline: Virus: attaches to a host file or boot sector, needs a user or program to run it, infects other files
Worm: standalone, spreads over the network by itself, no host file needed
Trojan: appears useful, relies on user trust, does not self-replicate
One example of payload for each and a note on propagation versus payload as separate ideas

bank.q: You are the security officer for an online examination portal at a mid-sized institute. Build a confidentiality determination matrix for five data items and three roles, and explain how you would use it during access-control reviews.
outline: Table with data items as rows and roles as columns
Each cell marked readable or not, with a stated condition where needed
Justification of at least two non-obvious decisions (for example, invigilator access to question papers only after the exam starts)
How the matrix becomes an access-control rule set and an audit checklist
Mention of what to do when a new role is created

bank.q: A retail website is hit by a flood of requests from thousands of home routers. Identify the attack, distinguish it from a single-source DoS, and describe the controls you would apply at the edge and at the application.
outline: Correctly names DDoS and explains amplification by botnet size
Distinguishes DoS (one source) from DDoS (many sources, harder to block by IP)
Edge controls: rate limiting, scrubbing centre, upstream filtering, anycast
Application controls: caching, CAPTCHA, connection timeouts, resource quotas
Mentions monitoring and a documented response plan

bank.q: Design an anti-phishing programme for a bank's customers and staff that pairs a user habit with a technical backstop. Explain why each part is needed.
outline: Awareness habit: verify sender domain, never act on links in urgent messages, report instead of clicking
Technical backstops: DMARC/SPF/DKIM on the bank's domain, mail filtering, link isolation, MFA that resists relayed codes
Recognition that training alone fails and technology alone fails
Reporting channel and a no-blame policy so staff report quickly
Measurement: click rates in simulations, time to report

bank.q: A student logs into a public Wi-Fi portal and then reaches the college email. Explain step by step how a man-in-the-middle attack and a replay attack would work here, and how TLS and a nonce or timestamp defeat them.
outline: MITM: rogue access point or ARP spoofing, attacker relays traffic, reads credentials
Replay: captured authentication message re-sent later
Why TLS with certificate validation stops MITM and why ignoring certificate warnings defeats it
Why random nonce or timestamp stops replay, and why sequence numbers alone are weaker
One line on HSTS and on not trusting open networks for sensitive logins

bank.q: Compare the CIA triad with the DAD triad. During a live DDoS on a power utility's billing site, which goal fails first and which goal should the response team protect at the cost of the others? Justify.
outline: Correct expansion of DAD: disclosure, alteration, destruction
Mapping of each DAD item to the CIA goal it breaks
Analysis showing availability fails first in a DDoS, while integrity and confidentiality remain intact
Argument for prioritising availability of the control system over billing, with a stated reason
Note that deliberately taking a service offline to preserve integrity is a valid trade-off

bank.q: A hospital asks you to rank its cyber risk. Using the relationship risk depends on threat, vulnerability and impact, evaluate three scenarios and justify a spending order.
outline: Explicit use of risk = likelihood × impact
Three concrete scenarios (ransomware on patient records, unpatched imaging device, phishing of staff)
Likelihood from threat exposure and known vulnerabilities, impact from patient safety and legal duty
Justified ranking with a lower-cost control for the highest risk first
Note that a low-likelihood, high-impact case still needs a contingency plan

bank.q: A vendor claims its signature-based antivirus alone is enough. Evaluate this claim against a polymorphic virus and ransomware, and propose a layered defence.
outline: Explains that a polymorphic virus changes its bytes, so signatures miss it
Ransomware often arrives through a user action and encrypts quickly, so detection time matters
Layer arguments: behaviour and heuristic detection, patching, least privilege, backup and restore testing, network segmentation
Evaluation of the vendor claim as necessary but not sufficient
Mentions the false-positive cost of aggressive detection

bank.q: An incident team sees 40,000 internal hosts contacting one external address every 30 seconds with small, similar-size packets. Analyse what this indicates, how jitter and beacon timing help or hinder detection, and how to respond.
outline: Identifies bots and a command-and-control channel with periodic beacons
Explains jitter as random delay added to beacon timing to avoid fixed-interval detection
Detection approaches: periodic-beacon analysis, DNS or flow records, threat intelligence matches, traffic size patterns
Response: block at the perimeter, isolate hosts, find the initial infection vector, preserve evidence
Warning that blocking one C2 address may push the botnet to a backup channel

bank.q: A manager says: 'We have a firewall and antivirus, so we are secure.' Evaluate this statement using the ideas of attack surface, threat, vulnerability and mechanism, and state what a sound security posture would add.
outline: Firewall and antivirus are mechanisms covering only part of the attack surface
Names uncovered surfaces: people (social engineering), remote access and botnet recruitment, unpatched software, wireless
Separation of threat, vulnerability, exposure and risk with a short example
Adds: patch management, MFA, least privilege, logging and monitoring, backups, incident response, user training
Concludes that security is a process with a stated threat model, not a product

glossary.def: Anything of value to the organisation — data, a service, a device, or its reputation.
The person, group or program that actually carries out a threat.
The state of being open to loss because a vulnerability exists and a threat can reach it.
Any safeguard — technical, procedural or physical — that reduces risk.
The path an attacker uses to reach a target, such as email attachment, open port or USB drive.
A maintained list of known threats, used as a checklist when analysing a system.
Common Weakness Enumeration; a dictionary of software weakness types rather than individual bugs.
Probing a range of ports on a host to learn which services are listening and therefore reachable.
Proving that a subject is who it claims to be, before any access is granted.
Being able to tie every action to an identified subject, so misuse can be traced.
The mechanism of transforming data with a key so unauthorised readers get nothing useful.
Malicious code that inserts itself into a host file or boot sector and runs when that host runs.
Self-contained malicious code that spreads across a network without a host file or user action.
A program that looks useful but carries hidden harmful function; it does not self-replicate.
Malicious code that stays dormant until a condition — a date, a login, a file change — is met.
A hidden way into a system that bypasses normal authentication, left by an attacker or a developer.
A single infected machine that takes orders from a remote operator.
The person who controls a botnet and rents or uses it.
The channel through which a botmaster sends instructions to bots and receives results.
A small periodic message a bot sends to its C2 server to ask for orders or report that it is alive.
Random variation added to beacon timing so the traffic does not look like a fixed clock.
Getting people to reveal information or perform actions by manipulating trust rather than breaking technology.
Leaving something tempting — a labelled USB stick, a free download — for the victim to pick up.
Following an authorised person through a door or gate without presenting credentials.
Offering a small favour or service in exchange for information or access.
Authorised simulated attack on a system to find exploitable weaknesses before an adversary does.
